inguinal-canal-relations: Locate the oblique passage The inguinal canal lies in the lower anterior abdominal wall above the medial portion of the inguinal ligament. Its deep ring opens in transversalis fascia, lateral to the inferior epigastric vessels. Its superficial ring opens in the external oblique aponeurosis near the pubic tubercle. Naming the fascial layer is more informative than simply saying that one ring is deeper, because the coverings and hernia routes follow these layers. Reconstruct four walls The anterior wall is chiefly external oblique aponeurosis, reinforced laterally by internal oblique. The posterior wall is chiefly transversalis fascia, reinforced medially by the conjoint tendon where present. The roof consists of arching fibres of internal oblique and transversus abdominis. The floor is formed by the inguinal ligament, with medial contribution from the lacunar ligament. These overlapping layers help explain why the canal is an oblique passage rather than a straight hole. Separate contents from the entry route The canal transmits the spermatic cord or the round ligament of the uterus. The ilioinguinal nerve travels through part of the canal and exits at the superficial ring, but does not enter through the deep ring. This is a useful exception to the tempting assumption that everything found in a canal must pass through both ends. When describing the cord, do not indiscriminately include every nearby nerve within its fascial contents. Use a fixed vascular landmark An indirect inguinal hernia enters the deep ring lateral to the inferior epigastric vessels and follows the canal. A direct inguinal hernia protrudes through the posterior wall medial to those vessels, in the inguinal triangle. The triangle is bounded by the lateral edge of rectus abdominis, the inferior epigastric vessels and the inguinal ligament. A femoral hernia uses a different route below the ligament; it should not be classified by borrowing the direct/indirect inguinal labels. Name both rings and the layers they pierce. Reconstruct the four walls. Classify the hernia route relative to the inferior epigastric vessels. Draw before naming On an internal-view sketch, a sac enters an opening lateral to the inferior epigastric vessels and then follows the inguinal canal. Identify its route. Label the inferior epigastric vessels first. The lateral opening is the deep inguinal ring. Entry there followed by passage through the canal describes an indirect inguinal route. An external bulge alone would not establish all these internal relationships.

Practice explaining a joint through its type, movement and stabilizers. Vertebral column & trunk Work through vertebral landmarks, the thoracic cage, diaphragm and abdominal wall. Organize the regions by boundaries, contents and relationships before rehearsing the hernia topics. Upper limb Follow the shoulder girdle through the arm and forearm to the hand. Connect spaces and compartments with their nerves and vessels, then revisit the brachial plexus and carpal tunnel. Pelvis & lower limb Begin with the hip-bone landmarks, then progress through hip stability, the gluteal region, thigh, knee, leg and foot. Trace the neurovascular routes as you move from region to region. Plexuses, skull & neck Bring the cervical, lumbar and sacral plexuses into the regional map. Review skull divisions, the temporomandibular joint, muscles of mastication and the neck muscle groups. Musculoskeletal development Link early embryology with limb, vertebral and skull development. Use the development topics to connect adult structures with their origins. Lymphatic drainage Organize drainage by territory and node group. Compare upper-limb, lower-limb, thoracic-wall and head-and-neck routes, then use the guide’s correction section to revisit common mix-ups. Oral-exam rehearsal Choose a topic, explain it aloud without looking, and check the answer framework. Use the guide’s 81 prompts and the decks’ closing drills to identify what needs another pass. Which three bones form each hip bone? The ilium, ischium and pubis meet at the acetabulum. What belongs inside the carpal tunnel? The median nerve and nine flexor tendons: four flexor digitorum superficialis, four flexor digitorum profundus and one flexor pollicis longus. The ulnar nerve and artery pass through Guyon’s canal; flexor carpi radialis has a separate tunnel, and palmaris longus lies superficial to the flexor retinaculum. How do flexion and extension relate to planes and axes? Flexion and extension occur in the sagittal plane around a transverse axis. Say the movement, plane and axis together when describing a joint.

thorax-nerve-relations: Find a reproducible landmark The sternal angle marks the manubriosternal junction and helps locate the second rib for rib counting. Its conventional transverse plane passes near the T4–T5 intervertebral level and divides the superior from the inferior mediastinum. These are orientation relationships; organ positions can vary with respiration, posture and individual anatomy. Place the nerves around the root The phrenic nerve passes anterior to the lung root, while the vagus passes posterior to it. The phrenic nerve continues towards the diaphragm and supplies its motor function. The vagus contributes to pulmonary and oesophageal autonomic networks. A simple anterior–posterior schematic teaches this relationship without reproducing the complete mediastinal course. Connect the diaphragm to function and development The phrenic nerves carry motor fibres principally from C3–C5. The diaphragm expands the thoracic cavity during inspiration and separates thoracic and abdominal compartments. Development involves several contributing structures, including the septum transversum and pleuroperitoneal membranes; its mature position should not be used to infer a thoracic origin for all its motor fibres. Lung-root nerve relationships Schematic showing the phrenic nerve anterior to the lung root and the vagus nerve posterior to it. Use the lung root as the landmark: phrenic anterior, vagus posterior. This is a relationship diagram, not a complete anatomical section or an image to use for procedural planning. Orient the two nerves at the lung root and connect one to its main motor target. The phrenic nerve runs anterior to the lung root and supplies the diaphragm through fibres principally from C3–C5. The vagus runs posterior to the root and contributes to thoracic autonomic networks. A diagram places the diaphragm low in the thorax. Why does this not imply thoracic motor roots? Its phrenic motor supply principally comes from C3–C5. Adult position and developmental history must be distinguished from segmental motor supply.
abdomen-portal-relations: Describe peritoneal relationships precisely Visceral peritoneum covers organs and parietal peritoneum lines the wall. Mesenteries connect selected organs to the wall and carry vessels, nerves and lymphatics. Intraperitoneal does not mean that an organ lies loose inside the fluid-filled peritoneal cavity: it describes its covering and attachment relationships. Locate the portal triad Within the hepatoduodenal ligament, the portal vein lies posterior to the bile duct and proper hepatic artery. Conventionally, the bile duct is on the patient's right and the proper hepatic artery on the left in the anterior pair. The supplied figure intentionally emphasises front–back order; its left–right arrangement is schematic. Connect rotation to adult position The embryonic gut tube lengthens, rotates and acquires different attachments. These changes help explain mesenteries and secondary retroperitoneal relationships. Foregut, midgut and hindgut divisions also organise major arterial territories. Arterial territory, peritoneal covering and venous drainage answer different questions and should not be used interchangeably. Portal triad: front-to-back relationships Diagram grouping the bile duct and hepatic artery anterior to the portal vein within the hepatoduodenal ligament. Distinguish front-to-back position from branching pattern: the portal vein is posterior; the bile duct and hepatic artery are anterior. Right and left are the patient’s. This simplified arrangement does not depict anatomical variation. Describe the portal triad while distinguishing the figure's main relationship from its simplification. The portal vein is posterior; the bile duct and proper hepatic artery are anterior. Conventionally the duct is right and artery left from the patient's perspective. The figure is a front–back relationship schematic rather than a complete operative view. In a conventional anterior view of the portal triad, where is the bile duct relative to the proper hepatic artery? On the patient's right. The duct conventionally lies to the patient's right of the proper hepatic artery; variants exist.
pelvis-urinary-route: Trace a continuous collecting route Urine leaving renal papillae enters minor calyces, then major calyces and the renal pelvis. The ureter transports it to the urinary bladder. The urethra carries urine from the bladder to the exterior. These are distinct segments; the ureter is not a continuation of the urethra, and blood follows a separate vascular route. Use relations to orient the ureter The ureters descend towards the pelvis and enter the bladder wall obliquely. In the female pelvis, the ureter passes beneath the uterine artery near the cervix. This is a relationship to recognise in anatomical study, not an instruction for locating or manipulating structures during a procedure. Connect support and development The pelvic diaphragm supports pelvic viscera and is mainly formed by levator ani and coccygeus. The urinary collecting system and renal nephrons have different embryological origins: the ureteric bud contributes the collecting system, while metanephric mesenchyme contributes nephrons. Their interaction connects two developing systems into a continuous urinary route. Two developmental partners in the kidney Flowchart distinguishing ureteric-bud derivatives in the collecting system from metanephric mesenchyme forming the nephron epithelium. Trace the two renal origins: ureteric bud to collecting system; metanephric mesenchyme to nephron epithelium. Their interaction is reciprocal. In the lower row, primordial germ cells migrate into the gonadal ridge; they are not produced by that ridge. Arrows summarise related processes, not every cell lineage. Connect the urinary route to its two renal developmental components. Nephrons derived from metanephric mesenchyme connect to the collecting system derived from the ureteric bud. Urine passes through collecting ducts to calyces, renal pelvis, ureter and bladder, then exits through the urethra. Which developmental pairing is correct? Ureteric bud forms the collecting system; metanephric mesenchyme forms nephrons. Reciprocal interaction between these tissues connects nephrons to the collecting system.
head-neck-tongue-map: Ask which sensory function is being tested For the anterior two-thirds of the tongue, general sensation mainly travels through the lingual nerve, a branch of V3. Taste from most of this region travels with chorda tympani fibres from VII that join the lingual nerve. Sharing part of a peripheral route does not make taste and general sensation the same cranial-nerve function. Check the posterior territory and the exception The glossopharyngeal nerve, IX, carries general sensation and taste from the posterior third. The circumvallate papillae lie just anterior to the terminal sulcus but receive taste innervation from IX. Sensory and taste fibres from the epiglottic region mainly travel through X. The regional figure is a useful summary but does not draw every boundary exception. Keep motor supply separate Most tongue muscles receive motor supply from XII. Palatoglossus is the major exception, receiving motor supply through the vagal pharyngeal plexus. Different developmental contributions to tongue regions help explain the mixed sensory map. An oral answer should name territory, modality and nerve before discussing a lesion. Tongue sensation and taste Tongue map showing anterior general sensation through V3, anterior taste through VII, posterior sensation and taste through IX, and epiglottic-region input through X. Separate general sensation from taste. Most anterior two-thirds general sensation travels in the lingual nerve (V3), while taste travels through chorda tympani (VII). Circumvallate papillae are the IX exception despite lying anterior to the sulcus terminalis. Motor supply is not shown. Explain why a single tongue map cannot replace a modality-specific answer. General sensation, taste and movement use different pathways. Most anterior general sensation uses V3, anterior taste uses VII, posterior sensation and taste use IX, and most motor supply uses XII. Circumvallate papillae and palatoglossus are important exceptions. Which exception should accompany an anterior-versus-posterior tongue taste map? Circumvallate papillae receive taste fibres from IX. Circumvallate papillae lie just anterior to the terminal sulcus but have IX taste innervation.
limbs-plexus-and-joints: Keep each plexus level distinct The usual brachial plexus begins with ventral rami C5–T1, then forms trunks, divisions, cords and terminal branches. The upper trunk usually combines C5–C6, the middle continues C7, and the lower combines C8–T1. Roots, trunks and cords are different organisational levels; the names should not be substituted for one another. Relate cords to an anatomical landmark Lateral, medial and posterior cords are named relative to the second part of the axillary artery. The musculocutaneous nerve arises from the lateral cord, the ulnar from the medial, and the axillary and radial from the posterior. The median nerve usually receives contributions from both lateral and medial cords. Normal anatomical variation should be expected. Explain movement using more than a nerve name A movement requires an appropriate muscle action, joint axis, intact nerve supply and mechanical conditions. Synovial joints have a cavity, capsule, articular surfaces and synovial lining; accessory structures vary. Developmental limb rotation helps explain adult compartment relationships, but a simplified plexus diagram does not show every muscle, cutaneous territory or variant branch. Brachial plexus: roots to terminal branches Flowchart tracing C5–T1 roots through trunks, divisions and cords to the main terminal nerves of the brachial plexus. Follow one route from roots to a terminal branch, then name the cords relative to the second part of the axillary artery. This organisational diagram omits collateral branches and individual variation. Trace C5–T1 through the plexus and explain how the cords are named. Ventral rami C5–T1 form upper, middle and lower trunks, each dividing into anterior and posterior divisions. These combine into lateral, medial and posterior cords, named relative to the second part of the axillary artery, and then give terminal branches. A diagram labels the posterior cord. Posterior relative to what? The second part of the axillary artery. The artery provides the conventional landmark for brachial-plexus cord names.
nitrogen-metabolism: Separate carbon from nitrogen Amino-acid metabolism handles two connected problems: use of the carbon skeleton and safe processing of nitrogen. Transamination transfers an amino group to a keto acid, commonly collecting nitrogen on glutamate. The carbon skeleton can enter other metabolic pathways. Transport and dispose Glutamine and alanine help transport nitrogen between tissues. The liver converts much waste nitrogen to urea through reactions spanning mitochondria and cytosol. The kidneys then excrete urea; hepatic production and renal elimination are distinct steps. Read the balance Nitrogen balance compares nitrogen intake with output. Positive balance can accompany net tissue growth; negative balance can accompany net tissue loss. It is an accounting concept whose interpretation depends on complete measurements and the physiological setting.
enzyme-kinetics: Change the route, not the equilibrium Enzymes lower the activation barrier and accelerate the approach to equilibrium. They do not change the equilibrium constant or make an unfavorable overall reaction favorable merely by being present. Coupling to another reaction is a different mechanism. Read a saturation curve In a simple Michaelis–Menten model, rate approaches Vmax as substrate rises. Km is the substrate concentration at half Vmax under that model. It is an operational kinetic parameter and should not automatically be equated with binding affinity in every mechanism. State the inhibition model For reversible competitive inhibition in the simple model, apparent Km rises while Vmax is unchanged. Pure noncompetitive inhibition lowers Vmax without changing Km. Mixed inhibition is more general; binding away from an active site alone does not prove pure noncompetitive behavior. Why can adding enzyme accelerate a reaction without changing its final equilibrium? Catalysis lowers the kinetic barrier for forward and reverse reaction paths. It changes how quickly equilibrium is reached, not the relative free energies of reactants and products. In a simple reversible competitive-inhibition model, what can increasing substrate concentration do? Reduce the inhibitor's effect on the observed rate. Substrate competes for binding; sufficiently high substrate can approach the same Vmax in the ideal model.
lipid-metabolism: Locate the synthesis machinery De novo fatty-acid synthesis occurs mainly in the cytosol. Acetyl-CoA carboxylase produces malonyl-CoA, which provides two-carbon building units for fatty-acid synthase. Elongation and desaturation also involve the endoplasmic reticulum. Supply reducing power Fatty-acid synthesis uses NADPH for reduction. This differs from pathways that oxidize fuel and generate NADH for respiratory-chain ATP production. Remember the direction of electron flow before treating NADH and NADPH as interchangeable abbreviations. Choose storage or structure Fatty acids can enter triacylglycerols for energy storage or membrane lipids for structural and signaling roles. Insulin and cellular energy state help coordinate synthesis with nutrient availability. A lipid molecule’s function depends on its complete molecular context.
glycolysis: Invest and recover ATP Cytosolic glycolysis converts one glucose to two pyruvate molecules. Two ATP are invested and four are produced by substrate-level phosphorylation, yielding a net two ATP. The pathway also reduces NAD+ to NADH. Regenerate the electron acceptor For glycolysis to continue, NAD+ must be available. Lactate dehydrogenase can reduce pyruvate to lactate while regenerating NAD+. Lactate formation does not itself add ATP; it supports continued ATP production by glycolysis. Connect tissues Lactate can leave a tissue and be used by another. In the Cori cycle, liver uses energy to make glucose from lactate. Recycling moves carbon between tissues and shifts the energy cost; it does not create free energy.
ketone-production-and-use: Follow the incoming fuel During fasting, the hormonal environment favours mobilisation of stored triacylglycerol. Released fatty acids travel to tissues, including liver, where mitochondrial beta-oxidation supplies acetyl-CoA and reducing equivalents. The acetyl-CoA has several possible fates. Its accumulation alone is not a complete explanation of ketosis: substrate supply, hepatic redox state and the availability of oxaloacetate for the citric-acid cycle all matter. Explain the hepatic branch point In liver mitochondria, acetyl-CoA can be channelled through HMG-CoA intermediates toward acetoacetate. Acetoacetate can be reduced to beta-hydroxybutyrate according to the mitochondrial redox state or contribute to acetone formation. Beta-hydroxybutyrate is grouped with ketone bodies physiologically even though it is not chemically a ketone. Mitochondrial ketogenesis should be distinguished from the cytosolic pathway using HMG-CoA in cholesterol synthesis. Ask which tissue can use the exported fuel Extrahepatic tissues with mitochondria can convert ketone bodies toward acetyl-CoA for oxidation. The liver lacks the key SCOT enzyme required for the usual ketolytic activation step and therefore exports rather than substantially consuming the ketone bodies it makes. Mature red blood cells lack mitochondria and cannot obtain ATP by ketone oxidation. The brain can increase ketone use during prolonged fasting, but this does not mean every tissue stops requiring glucose. Interpret fuel patterns in context Ketone production is part of fasting adaptation, but markedly abnormal accumulation can occur in other metabolic settings. A measured ketone result alone does not establish its cause or acid–base consequence. In a mechanistic answer, name production, transport, tissue uptake and oxidation separately. Avoid the misleading statement that fatty acids become net glucose through acetyl-CoA: the even-chain fatty-acid acetyl units do not provide net glucose in humans, although glycerol and odd-chain contributions are separate cases. Trace fatty acids toward hepatic ketogenesis. Explain why liver and red cells cannot use ketones in the same way as other tissues. Distinguish physiological fuel adaptation from a diagnosis. Compare two tissues A fictional fasting model delivers labelled beta-hydroxybutyrate to heart muscle and mature red blood cells. Which can use its carbon for mitochondrial ATP production? Heart muscle has mitochondria and ketolytic capacity, so it can oxidise the ketone carbon. Mature red cells have no mitochondria and rely on glycolysis for ATP. A circulating fuel can be available to both cells without being usable by both.
lipoprotein-routes: Start with the packaging problem Triacylglycerols and cholesteryl esters are poorly soluble in plasma. Lipoprotein particles package hydrophobic cargo inside a surface containing phospholipids, free cholesterol and apolipoproteins. A particle is not simply cholesterol with a different name. Its size, composition and apolipoproteins affect transport and recognition. Plasma cholesterol measurements describe transported lipid; they are not direct counts of all particles or a complete account of their metabolism. Follow the intestinal route Enterocytes assemble chylomicrons carrying much of the absorbed dietary lipid. In capillary beds, lipoprotein lipase hydrolyses particle triacylglycerol so fatty acids can be taken up by tissues. ApoC-II supports this enzyme interaction. After substantial triacylglycerol removal, chylomicron remnants are taken up by the liver through pathways involving apoE. The enzyme that removes lipid cargo and the receptor that removes a remnant are different steps. Follow the hepatic route The liver secretes VLDL to export triacylglycerol. Lipid removal and remodelling generate remnant particles, including IDL, with some continuing toward LDL. LDL is relatively enriched in cholesterol and contains apoB-100, which participates in LDL-receptor recognition. Receptor-mediated endocytosis brings the particle into the cell, where components are processed. The sequence is not that VLDL is manufactured by the intestine or that LDL is the same thing as a free cholesterol molecule. Place HDL in a transport network HDL participates in cholesterol movement from peripheral cells and in exchange and delivery processes that involve other particles and liver. LCAT esterifies cholesterol on HDL, supporting movement into its hydrophobic core. This is a network with multiple pathways, not a one-way vacuum cleaner. Familiar good and bad labels can obscure the mechanisms. For an oral answer, track origin, dominant cargo, key processing step and destination, then discuss any measurement separately. Follow chylomicrons and VLDL from their organs of origin. Distinguish lipoprotein lipase from an uptake receptor. Explain why particle identity changes as cargo is removed. Find the blocked step In a fictional model, triglyceride-rich particles enter blood normally but capillary lipoprotein-lipase activity is markedly reduced. Predict the immediate transport problem. Hydrolysis of particle triacylglycerol is impaired. Delivery of fatty acids through this pathway falls and triglyceride-rich particles persist longer. This is a processing defect, not proof that intestinal particle synthesis or LDL-receptor binding has failed.
protein-structure: Start with the sequence A protein’s primary structure is its amino-acid sequence. Side-chain charge, hydrophobicity and geometry influence interactions with water and neighboring residues. Ionizable groups change protonation with pH, so charge is contextual rather than a permanent label for the whole protein. Build the folded structure Local backbone arrangements form secondary structure. Tertiary structure describes the overall fold of one polypeptide; quaternary structure describes association of multiple subunits. Disrupting folding can impair function without changing the original amino-acid sequence. Use collagen as an example Collagen assembly requires a characteristic triple-helical organization and post-translational processing. Hydroxylation and later extracellular cross-linking support stability. Its role in matrix connects molecular structure to the tensile behavior of connective tissues.
pdh-tca: Cross the pyruvate gate The pyruvate dehydrogenase complex converts pyruvate to acetyl-CoA, releasing CO2 and producing NADH. This oxidative decarboxylation is effectively irreversible in human metabolism. It links glycolytic carbon to mitochondrial oxidation. Follow the cycle Acetyl-CoA combines with oxaloacetate to form citrate. Subsequent reactions regenerate oxaloacetate while producing reduced electron carriers, CO2 and a substrate-level phosphorylation product. Oxaloacetate is a regenerated acceptor, yet withdrawal of intermediates requires replenishment. Separate coupled processes NADH and FAD-linked reducing equivalents support respiratory-chain electron transfer. Oxygen is the terminal electron acceptor of that chain, not a direct substrate in each TCA reaction. Sustained oxidative flux nevertheless depends on reoxidation of the reduced carriers.
biophysics-dosimetry: Separate units Activity in Bq counts decays per second; absorbed dose D in gray is energy deposited per mass, with 1 Gy = 1 J/kg. Exposure is a charge-per-mass quantity defined for photon ionisation in air, not a general tissue dose. No universal Bq-to-Gy conversion exists without geometry, energies, time and biokinetics. Explain weighting Equivalent dose weights organ absorbed dose for radiation type. Effective dose additionally combines tissue-weighted contributions as a protection quantity. Both use sieverts, but identical units do not make them interchangeable with gray or with an individual patient's predicted injury. Weighting factors belong to a specified protection framework. Follow damage pathways Radiation can affect a target directly or indirectly through chemical species produced in surrounding material, notably water. Physical interactions precede chemical and biological responses. Tissue reactions and stochastic effects have different dose–response concepts. A dose number alone omits distribution, dose rate and biological context. Use protection principles Justification asks whether an exposure is warranted; optimisation seeks an appropriate balance while limiting unnecessary exposure. Time, distance and suitable shielding alter exposure pathways. Dose limits in regulated exposure categories are not interchangeable with patient medical exposures, and current local requirements must be checked separately. Work energy per mass If 0.02 J is deposited uniformly in 0.10 kg, absorbed dose is 0.20 Gy. Without radiation type and distribution this result cannot be relabelled as effective dose. Doubling mass at the same deposited energy halves absorbed dose; doubling activity alone does not determine the dose change.
biophysics-absorption-scattering: Track the missing beam A detector placed directly behind a sample measures transmitted light. Reduced transmission can reflect absorption, scattering out of the beam or reflection. Only absorbed energy is necessarily transferred internally to the sample. Geometry and collection optics determine whether scattered light contributes to the measured signal. Apply Beer–Lambert carefully For a homogeneous non-scattering dilute solution under suitable monochromatic conditions, A = log₁₀(I₀/I) = εcl. Absorbance is dimensionless, c is concentration and l is path length; ε must use compatible units. A blank corrects for solvent and container contributions, not for every possible sample artifact. Explain spectral structure Molecules absorb when photon energy matches allowed electronic, vibrational or rotational transitions. A spectrometer separates wavelengths and measures a response across them. Broad molecular bands differ from isolated atomic lines. Peaks alone may not identify a compound uniquely, especially when several absorbing species overlap. Compare scattering Rayleigh scattering applies to particles much smaller than wavelength and has a strong inverse wavelength dependence. Mie scattering describes larger spherical-particle regimes with more complex angular behaviour. Dynamic light scattering analyses fluctuations caused by particle motion, linking correlation times to diffusion under a model rather than directly photographing particle diameters. Work a transmission result If I/I₀ = 0.01, absorbance is 2. Increasing concentration twofold at fixed ε and l predicts A = 4, or transmission 0.0001. Such tiny signals may exceed useful instrument range because stray light and noise matter. A linear equation does not guarantee reliable measurements at arbitrary concentration.
biophysics-action-potentials: Start with positive feedback In a typical axon, sufficient depolarisation activates voltage-gated inward current, producing further depolarisation. Threshold marks a balance where regenerative activation can outpace opposing processes. The detailed channel types and waveform vary among excitable cells, so a neuronal sodium spike is not every action potential. Follow recovery Sodium-channel inactivation and delayed outward potassium current help repolarise a typical axon. Refractoriness reflects channel state and conductances: during an absolute refractory interval, another normal spike cannot be triggered; during a relative interval, excitability is reduced. It is not simply that all ions have been used up. Explain propagation Local circuit currents depolarise adjacent membrane, where new regenerative current develops. The passive current spreads with decrement, but a normal propagated action potential is repeatedly renewed rather than exponentially shrinking along the entire axon. Refractory membrane behind the front supports forward progression after initiation. Compare fibre properties Increasing diameter reduces internal resistance and can increase conduction speed. Myelin reduces current leakage and effective membrane charging requirements between nodes; regeneration occurs at nodes of Ranvier. Saltatory conduction does not mean ions leap through empty space from one node to the next. Connect to recording An intracellular voltage and a surface extracellular potential are different measurements. Surface signals depend on spatial current distributions, orientation and volume conduction. Stronger stimulation often changes recruitment or firing rate rather than increasing the height of each all-or-none spike in one healthy axon.
biophysics-atomic-models: Follow the evidence Dalton's atom model organised chemical composition; Thomson introduced embedded electrons; scattering experiments required a small concentrated positive nucleus. A classical planetary electron would radiate and collapse, so it cannot explain stable atomic structure. Model revision follows a failed prediction, not simply a more detailed drawing. Quantise energy Bohr's hydrogen model allows selected energies and photons with hf = |ΔE| between levels. It explains important hydrogen spectral features but does not supply a general picture of multi-electron atoms. The quantum model uses orbitals as probability distributions, not narrow tracks traversed by miniature planets. Use quantum numbers Principal, angular-momentum, magnetic and spin quantum numbers organise electron states. Pauli exclusion prevents two electrons in an atom from sharing the full set. Shell filling, effective nuclear charge and shielding help explain periodic chemical properties. An orbital's spatial extent is different from a measured instantaneous electron position. Interpret uncertainty The relation Δx Δp ≥ ħ/2 constrains a state's position and momentum spreads. It is not merely a poor microscope or a statement that electrons have no measurable properties. Wave packets require a range of momenta to localise a particle; tighter localisation broadens that distribution. Read experimental transitions In a Franck–Hertz-type experiment, electrons lose discrete amounts of energy when exciting atoms. A 5 eV excitation would correspond to a photon of roughly 248 nm if the atom returned directly by emitting one photon. Multiple allowed decay pathways can produce several spectral lines instead.
biophysics-signals: Classify the information Signals may be continuous or discrete in time, analogue or quantised in amplitude, periodic or aperiodic. A biological process must first be converted into a measurable quantity by a transducer. Distinguish the original signal from the displayed trace, which has already passed through sensors and processing. Read time and frequency Amplitude describes size; frequency describes repetition rate. Fourier analysis represents suitable signals as combinations of frequency components. A short pulse contains a broad frequency range. Changing a waveform's shape can therefore change its spectrum even when the main repetition period is unchanged. Explain filtering and amplification Low-pass filters attenuate higher frequencies; high-pass filters attenuate lower ones; band-pass filters select a range. Amplification scales signals but also acts on noise within its bandwidth. Filtering can remove interference and also distort meaningful features, so cutoffs must relate to the physiological question. Sample without inventing detail For a band-limited signal, the sampling rate must exceed twice the highest frequency to avoid aliasing under ideal reconstruction assumptions. An analogue anti-alias filter acts before sampling. Quantisation maps amplitudes into discrete levels; more bits reduce the step size for a fixed range but do not cure sensor noise. Work a sampling choice A signal restricted below 100 Hz needs a sampling rate above 200 samples/s, with practical margin for real filters. Sampling at 150 samples/s can misrepresent high-frequency content as lower-frequency variation. Upsampling that record later cannot recover information already aliased at acquisition.
biophysics-thermal-radiation: Define an ideal reference A blackbody absorbs incident radiation completely and emits a temperature-dependent equilibrium spectrum. Real surfaces are described using emissivity, which can depend on wavelength, angle and temperature. A dark appearance in visible light does not automatically imply identical behaviour in thermal infrared. Read the laws together Planck's law gives the spectral distribution. Wien's wavelength displacement law gives λmax T ≈ 2.898 × 10⁻³ m·K. Stefan–Boltzmann gives total blackbody radiant exitance M = σT⁴. The peak location and total area describe different aspects of one spectrum; use kelvin in both relations. Account for surroundings For an idealised grey surface exchanging radiation with a large enclosure, net power is approximately εσA(T⁴ − Tenv⁴). Emission alone is not net cooling because the body also absorbs radiation. Kirchhoff's relation links emissivity and absorptivity at thermal equilibrium under corresponding spectral and directional conditions. Work a thermal scale At 300 K, Wien's relation gives a peak near 9.7 μm, in the infrared. Doubling absolute temperature multiplies ideal total emitted power per area by 16 and halves peak wavelength. A small rise around body temperature is not equivalent to doubling kelvin temperature. Interpret an image A thermal camera estimates apparent surface temperature from detected infrared radiation and assumptions about emissivity and surroundings. Reflections, sweat, coverings and environment affect readings. The image represents surface radiance, not a direct map of deep internal temperature or a diagnosis by colour alone.
biophysics-molecular-interactions: Read an energy curve A stable separation lies near a potential-energy minimum where net force is zero and curvature is positive. Attraction dominates over one distance range and steep repulsion prevents unlimited approach. Force is the negative spatial derivative of potential energy: zero potential is not the same thing as zero force. Compare chemical interactions Covalent bonding involves shared electron density; ionic interactions involve charges and depend strongly on the medium. Electronegativity differences help predict bond polarity. Hydrogen bonds are directional interactions involving suitable donors and acceptors. Dispersion forces occur even in nonpolar molecules through fluctuating charge distributions. Connect many weak interactions Thermal energy kBT competes with interaction energies. Individually modest noncovalent contacts can stabilise a large macromolecule when many act together. Solvent and entropy affect the free-energy balance, so counting bonds alone does not predict whether a complex forms. Hydrophobic association is a solvent-related effect rather than a new covalent bond. Measure surfaces Scanning tunnelling microscopy senses a tunnelling current that depends sharply on tip–sample separation and electronic states, requiring a suitable conducting pathway. Atomic force microscopy senses tip forces through a cantilever and can study insulating samples. Neither instrument produces an ordinary colour photograph of atoms. Predict a perturbation Moving particles slightly away from a stable minimum produces a restoring tendency. Raising temperature may increase fluctuations enough to disrupt weak associations, but no single temperature applies to every interaction. For a probe image, ask whether apparent height reflects topography, electronic structure or the chosen force-feedback mode.
biophysics-respiratory-physics: Separate the pressures Airflow depends on pressure difference between airway opening and alveoli. Transpulmonary pressure is alveolar minus pleural pressure and helps describe lung distension. It is not the pressure across the chest wall. Pleural pressure is normally subatmospheric during quiet breathing but need not always be negative. Follow a quiet breath Inspiratory muscle activity expands the thorax, changes pleural pressure and expands the lung; alveolar pressure falls slightly below atmospheric pressure during inward flow. Quiet expiration is mainly passive recoil. At moments of zero flow, alveolar pressure may equal atmospheric pressure even though the lung remains expanded. Define the volumes Tidal volume is the volume of an ordinary breath. Residual volume remains after maximal expiration. Functional residual capacity is the volume after an ordinary passive expiration: expiratory reserve volume plus residual volume. Spirometry alone cannot directly measure residual volume or capacities containing it. Connect mechanics and exchange Compliance is ΔV/ΔP over a specified range; resistance opposes flow. Restrictive and obstructive processes affect these differently. Henry's law links dissolved gas concentration to partial pressure through a gas–liquid-specific coefficient. Diffusion, ventilation and perfusion all contribute to exchange, so no single volume establishes adequate gas transfer. Interpret examination physics Inspection observes motion; palpation senses mechanical transmission; percussion probes the response of tissue and air-containing structures to an impulse; auscultation listens to sound generated and transmitted through the system. None gives a unique diagnosis from one sound. If ERV = 1.0 L and RV = 1.2 L, FRC = 2.2 L.
biophysics-circulation-ecg: Follow pressure and resistance Flow is driven by a pressure difference and limited by vascular resistance. Mean pressure falls along the systemic circuit, with major regulation in resistance vessels. A pressure value at one point does not by itself determine flow; the downstream pressure and resistance also matter. Explain the Windkessel effect Elastic large arteries store some energy during ejection and release it during diastole, smoothing flow. This compliance effect is distinct from active cardiac pumping. Total cross-sectional area changes through the network, so mean speed need not follow pressure with the same spatial pattern. Read a pressure–volume loop Ventricular filling, isovolumetric contraction, ejection and isovolumetric relaxation form an idealised cycle. The enclosed loop area represents external pressure–volume work per beat. Stroke volume is the difference between end-diastolic and end-systolic volumes, not the absolute volume at either corner. Connect electrical sequence The ECG records body-surface potential differences generated by cardiac electrical activity. P, QRS and T relate broadly to atrial depolarisation, ventricular depolarisation and ventricular repolarisation. Mechanical contraction follows electrical activation but is not directly drawn as voltage. Lead orientation affects waveform size and polarity. Work two checks For a simplified mean ejection pressure of 100 mmHg and stroke volume 70 mL, pressure times volume is roughly 0.93 J, an approximation to external work. For ideal limb-lead voltages with consistent sign convention, lead II = lead I + lead III. Check calibration before converting millimetres into time or millivolts.
biophysics-fluid-flow: Conserve volume For steady incompressible flow, Q = Av and the same volume flow passes successive cross-sections without leaks. A smaller total area therefore means greater mean speed at fixed Q. In a branching network, use the sum of parallel cross-sectional areas rather than comparing only one small vessel with one large vessel. Distinguish ideal and viscous descriptions Bernoulli's equation relates pressure, speed and height along an ideal steady streamline without dissipative losses. Real viscous flow loses mechanical energy. Newtonian shear stress obeys τ = η dv/dy. Blood's apparent viscosity depends on flow conditions and cellular content, so it is not a universal constant. Use Poiseuille's law For steady fully developed laminar flow of a Newtonian fluid in a rigid circular tube, Q = πr⁴Δp/(8ηL). Resistance is 8ηL/(πr⁴). Radius has a strong fourth-power effect. Pulsatile blood vessels with flexible walls and non-Newtonian behaviour depart from this exact model. Compare regimes and drag Reynolds number Re = ρvD/η compares inertial and viscous tendencies; geometry and disturbances affect transition. Stokes drag F = 6πηrv applies to a small sphere at low Reynolds number. Plasma skimming and cell distribution at branches can change local blood composition as well as flow. Work a radius change At fixed pressure difference, length and viscosity, doubling radius predicts 16 times the flow. At fixed flow, the same change reduces the required pressure difference to one sixteenth. These are different experimental constraints; always state what is held constant.
biophysics-decay-interactions: Use the decay law For one radionuclide, N(t) = N₀exp(−λt) and activity A(t) = λN(t). Activity is measured in becquerels, meaning decays per second. Half-life T½ = ln 2/λ and mean lifetime τ = 1/λ are different. Individual decays are random even though large populations follow a predictable statistical curve. Track charged particles Alpha particles produce dense ionisation over a short range. Electrons and positrons lose energy through interactions with matter; positrons eventually annihilate with electrons, commonly producing two approximately 511 keV photons. Fast protons have a depth-dependent energy deposition with a Bragg peak near the end of their range. Distinguish photon mechanisms Photoelectric absorption transfers photon energy to an electron, with binding-energy bookkeeping. Compton scattering transfers some energy to an electron and leaves a redirected lower-energy photon. Pair production requires at least 1.022 MeV near a suitable interaction partner, producing an electron and positron. Apply attenuation A narrow monoenergetic photon beam can follow I = I₀exp(−μx) through a uniform absorber. Attenuation includes photons removed by scattering as well as absorption. Its coefficient depends on energy and material; it is not a universal percentage per centimetre. Neutrons interact chiefly with nuclei rather than by direct electric ionisation. Work a time example An 800 Bq sample with a 2-hour half-life has expected activity 100 Bq after 6 hours: three half-lives leave one eighth. This does not mean every original nucleus survived exactly two hours. A detector count rate also depends on efficiency, geometry and background.
biophysics-radiation-detection: Convert an event A scintillator converts some deposited energy into light. A photomultiplier converts that light into photoelectrons and amplifies their number through dynodes. Pulse height can track deposited energy under calibrated conditions; pulse count tracks detected events. Neither is automatically equal to source activity. Compare gas detectors An ionisation chamber collects primary ionisation charge. A proportional counter uses gas multiplication while retaining information about initial ionisation. In a Geiger–Müller tube, avalanches make pulse sizes largely independent of incident energy, so it is useful for counting but not ordinary pulse-height energy spectroscopy. Use semiconductor detectors Energy deposition creates electron–hole pairs that can be collected as charge. Detector material, thickness, noise and energy resolution affect performance. A discriminator rejects pulses below a threshold, reducing some noise but potentially rejecting genuine events. Calibration is needed to associate a channel number with an energy. Interpret counts statistically For independent Poisson events, the standard deviation of N counts is approximately √N. Relative counting uncertainty is about 1/√N. Background subtraction introduces uncertainty from both measurements. Dead time causes missed events at high rates, so observed counts need not rise linearly without limit. Work precision and gain Collecting 10,000 counts gives about 1% counting uncertainty before other errors, compared with 10% for 100 counts. Eight ideal dynodes each multiplying electrons by 3 give gain 3⁸ = 6561. Gain increases pulse amplitude, not the number of radioactive decays occurring in the sample.
biophysics-diffusion-osmosis: Start from random motion Brownian motion is irregular motion driven by molecular impacts. Net diffusion emerges statistically from concentration differences, not from molecules intentionally seeking dilute regions. Fick's first law J = −D dc/dx expresses flux down a gradient, with the minus sign indicating direction. Follow time dependence Fick's second law describes how concentration changes as diffusion redistributes material. In one dimension, mean squared displacement is 2Dt for free diffusion. Typical diffusion time therefore grows with distance squared. Diffusion is effective over short cellular distances but rapidly becomes slow across much larger distances. Relate size and transport For a sphere in a suitable dilute fluid, Stokes–Einstein gives D = kBT/(6πηr). Higher temperature tends to increase D, while greater viscosity or particle radius reduces it in this model. Binding, crowding and membranes can make transport in tissue differ from free diffusion. Explain osmotic and thermal driving Osmosis is solvent movement associated with a chemical-potential difference across a selectively permeable boundary. For ideal dilute solutions, osmotic pressure is approximately cRT for solute particle concentration c. Fourier's heat law has a similar gradient form, with heat flux proportional to negative temperature gradient; thermodiffusion couples temperature and material transport. Work a distance comparison If diffusion across 10 μm takes a characteristic time t, crossing 100 μm under the same conditions takes roughly 100t. In alveolar exchange, area, barrier thickness and partial-pressure gradients influence transfer. Convection brings gases to the exchange surface; diffusion carries them across the thin barrier.
biophysics-entropy-potentials: Interpret the second law For an isolated system, total entropy cannot decrease in a spontaneous process. A subsystem can become more ordered while exporting heat or matter, so local order does not violate the second law. Biological organisation requires an energy and entropy balance with the surroundings rather than a claim that organisms escape thermodynamics. Connect microscopic and macroscopic views Boltzmann entropy S = kB ln Ω links multiplicity with entropy for an appropriate statistical description. For a reversible heat transfer, dS = δQrev/T. Irreversible processes generate entropy. The third law concerns entropy as temperature approaches absolute zero under specified conditions; it does not say ordinary biological entropy is zero. Choose a potential Helmholtz free energy F = U − TS is useful at fixed temperature and volume. Gibbs free energy G = H − TS, with H = U + pV, is useful at fixed temperature and pressure. Under appropriate closed-system constraints, spontaneous change lowers the relevant potential toward equilibrium. Separate favourability and rate A negative reaction ΔG indicates thermodynamic favourability in the specified state, not a fast reaction. Activation barriers determine kinetics. Concentrations affect ΔG through chemical potentials, so a standard free-energy value alone does not specify the direction under every cellular condition. Coupling can make a combined process favourable. Work a balance At fixed temperature and pressure, let ΔH = 20 kJ/mol and TΔS = 30 kJ/mol. Then ΔG = −10 kJ/mol, despite positive enthalpy change. If the entropy contribution changes with conditions, the result may differ. State units consistently and do not multiply a Celsius value into TΔS.
biophysics-luminescence: Build an energy diagram Absorption promotes a molecule into an excited state. Vibrational relaxation and internal conversion can reduce its energy without photon emission. Fluorescence commonly occurs from the lowest excited singlet state to the ground state, consistent with Kasha's rule in many molecules. Exceptions exist, so the rule is not an absolute prohibition. Distinguish delayed emission Intersystem crossing changes spin multiplicity and can populate a triplet state. Phosphorescence commonly involves a spin-forbidden triplet-to-singlet transition and is often longer lived than fluorescence. Both are luminescence; neither requires a body to have the blackbody temperature corresponding to the emitted colour. Measure yield and lifetime Quantum yield is emitted photons divided by absorbed photons. Lifetime describes excited-state population decay, often approximately exponential. Nonradiative pathways reduce yield and can shorten lifetime. Intensity also depends on illumination, concentration, collection and detector response, so dim emission alone does not uniquely identify the cause. Separate excitation from detection A fluorimeter selects excitation and observes emission with spectral separation, often using a right-angle geometry to reduce direct excitation light. Fluorescence microscopy uses labels and filters to localise signals. A Stokes shift places common emission at longer wavelength than excitation because some energy is lost before photon emission. Work a decay For a single lifetime τ = 4 ns, the excited population remaining after 4 ns is e⁻¹ ≈ 37%. A 40% quantum yield means about 40 emitted photons per 100 absorbed on average, not that every molecule emits a photon with 40% of the excitation energy.
biophysics-nuclear-imaging: Localise single photons A gamma camera uses a collimator to restrict photon directions, a detector to register events and electronics to estimate position and energy. Collimation improves spatial information but rejects many photons. A planar image combines depth information in projection; rotating views support SPECT reconstruction. Localise annihilation events PET detects near-coincident photons from positron annihilation and assigns a line of response between detectors. Many such events support reconstruction. Positron range, non-collinearity, scatter and random coincidences affect resolution and accuracy. PET measures a tracer distribution, not a direct photograph of every metabolic reaction. Combine modalities PET/CT and SPECT/CT combine functional tracer information with anatomical localisation and attenuation correction. Registration errors can arise from motion or mismatched acquisition conditions. Hybrid imaging does not remove the distinct limitations of each component; the physical origin of each image should remain clear. Shape therapeutic dose External-beam therapy directs radiation from outside; brachytherapy places sources near or within a treatment region. Multiple beam directions and collimation can concentrate dose geometrically. Charged-particle range and photon depth-dose behaviour differ. Planning must balance target coverage and surrounding tissues rather than assuming one beam only affects its target. Reason about sensitivity Narrower collimator acceptance commonly improves directional selection while reducing detected counts. More counts can improve statistical precision but are not equivalent to better intrinsic spatial resolution. Draw a line of response for PET and a collimated ray for a gamma camera to explain why their localisation mechanisms differ.
biophysics-gases-statistics: Connect microscopic motion to pressure Gas pressure comes from momentum transfer in collisions with container walls. For a dilute ideal gas, pV = NkBT = nRT. Absolute temperature is required. The model neglects molecular volume and intermolecular potential energy; high density and proximity to condensation make those assumptions unreliable. Describe speeds statistically A Maxwell–Boltzmann distribution describes speeds in a classical equilibrium gas. Molecules do not all share the mean speed. Raising temperature broadens the distribution and shifts characteristic speeds upward; heavier particles have lower characteristic speeds at the same temperature. Mean translational energy is 3kBT/2 per particle. Compare energy populations For equal degeneracy, relative occupation of two states is exp(−ΔE/kBT). Larger energy gaps reduce high-energy occupation, while warming makes it less strongly suppressed. Barometric density variation is a spatial version of this balance in gravity. Degeneracy must be included when states have unequal multiplicity. Recognise nonideal behaviour The van der Waals equation introduces finite molecular volume and attractive forces. These corrections explain why an ideal-gas extrapolation can fail. At equilibrium chemical reactions balance forward and reverse rates; Arrhenius temperature dependence describes barrier crossing, not proof that every collision reacts. Work and interpret An ideal gas warmed from 300 K to 330 K at fixed volume has pressure multiplied by 330/300 = 1.10. Celsius temperatures would give the wrong ratio. Entropy S = kB ln Ω connects accessible microstates with bulk thermodynamics, but Ω must refer to states consistent with the specified macroscopic constraints.
biophysics-wave-optics: Track phase A harmonic oscillation repeats with frequency f and period 1/f. A travelling wave obeys v = fλ. Superposition adds amplitudes, including their signs and phases: equal coherent waves can reinforce or cancel. Stable interference requires a sufficiently stable phase relationship, not merely two beams of the same colour. Explain diffraction Huygens–Fresnel reasoning treats each part of a wavefront as contributing secondary waves. A finite aperture spreads light; narrowing it generally broadens the diffraction pattern. For a grating at normal incidence, d sin θ = mλ locates principal maxima. Different wavelengths therefore emerge at different angles. Distinguish resolution from magnification A common microscope estimate is d ≈ 0.61λ/NA, where NA = n sin α and α is the collection half-angle. Shorter wavelength or larger numerical aperture reduces the resolvable spacing. This is a model-dependent criterion, not a promise that every specimen will show that detail despite noise and poor contrast. Use polarisation and phase Linear polarisation specifies the electric-field orientation. An ideal analyser transmits intensity I = I₀ cos²θ for linearly polarised input. Birefringent material gives different phase delays to orthogonal components. A phase-contrast microscope converts specimen phase differences into visible intensity differences, enabling observation of weakly absorbing structures. Work a comparison At fixed NA, changing illumination from 600 nm to 450 nm reduces the estimated resolution distance to 450/600 = 0.75 of its former value. A stronger eyepiece alone does not change this distance. Draw both the specimen spacing and diffraction spots before claiming that two points are resolved.
biophysics-image-formation: Choose a sign convention For a thin lens in air, use 1/f = 1/u + 1/v with u positive for a real object and v positive for a real image on the outgoing side. A converging lens has positive f. State the convention before interpreting a negative value; diagrams and equations must describe the same geometry. Construct the image Trace a parallel ray through the far focus and a central ray approximately undeviated. An object beyond f gives a real inverted image; one inside f gives a virtual upright enlarged image. Exactly at f the emerging rays are parallel. A virtual image is located by backward extensions and cannot be caught directly on a screen. Combine optical elements Power P = 1/f in metres is measured in dioptres. Powers add for thin lenses in contact, but separation changes the equivalent system. A microscope objective forms an enlarged intermediate image; an eyepiece acts as a magnifier. Total nominal magnification is the product, whereas resolution depends on wavelength and numerical aperture. Calculate an image For f = 10 cm and u = 30 cm, 1/v = 1/10 − 1/30, so v = 15 cm. Magnification m = −v/u = −0.5: the real image is inverted and half the object height. The lens power is +10 D, because f = 0.10 m. Connect to the eye The cornea and lens focus a real inverted image on the retina. Accommodation changes lens power; it does not move a screen-like retina. Spherical and chromatic aberrations are departures from the ideal thin-lens model. Enlarging an already blurred image adds size without recovering lost spatial information.
biophysics-resting-potential: Build an electrochemical balance An ion moves under both concentration and electrical influences. For one permeant ion at equilibrium, the Nernst equation gives E = RT/(zF) ln(coutside/cinside) using inside potential relative to outside. The sign depends on valence as well as the concentration ratio. Equilibrium for one ion need not mean zero current for every ion. Use selective permeability The resting membrane potential reflects gradients and relative permeabilities. The Goldman–Hodgkin–Katz voltage equation extends the comparison to several permeant monovalent ions under its assumptions, with anion concentrations appearing in reversed positions. Pumps maintain gradients over time; the voltage is not simply a direct count of pump cycles. Model electrical storage A membrane separates charge and behaves capacitively, while conducting pathways provide resistance. An elementary RC model has time constant τ = RC. After one time constant, a charging response has completed about 63% of its final change. This does not mean ions have all reached their equilibrium distributions. Explain spatial spread and Donnan effects Passive voltage changes decay along a leaky cable; length constant describes the distance over which amplitude falls to 1/e in a simple model. Regenerative action potentials are different. Impermeant charged solutes can create Donnan ion distributions and osmotic effects, constrained in cells by pumps and volume regulation. Work a Nernst estimate For K⁺ at about 37°C with outside/inside concentration ratio 0.1, E is approximately −61.5 mV. Increasing outside K⁺ makes that equilibrium potential less negative. Predict the direction before calculating, and distinguish this single-ion value from a full resting-potential estimate.
biophysics-molecular-motors: Identify motor functions Myosin, kinesin and dynein convert chemical free energy into coordinated mechanical steps. Processivity describes how many steps a motor can take before detaching, not simply its maximum speed. Load, ATP availability and track properties influence motion. Thermal fluctuations coexist with directed molecular transport. Explain sliding filaments Muscle shortening arises from relative sliding of actin and myosin, not wholesale shortening of the filaments. Cross-bridge attachment, force generation and detachment form a cycle coupled to ATP chemistry. Calcium regulation makes suitable binding interactions available; ATP is also needed for detachment. Compare contraction conditions Isometric means fixed overall muscle length; isotonic describes an idealised constant-load condition. External mechanical work is force times displacement along the force direction, so a strictly isometric contraction performs no external shortening work despite consuming energy. Internal processes and heat production continue. Read force and timing Repeated activation can sum twitches and, in suitable muscle, produce tetanus. Force–velocity behaviour links shortening speed to load; maximum shortening speed is not the point of maximum power because power also requires force. Muscle length affects overlap and force-generating capacity. Work and interpret A constant 20 N force moving a load 0.05 m performs 1 J of work. At zero displacement external work is zero even if tension is 20 N. Compare this with energy consumed rather than equating mechanical output with every ATP molecule's free-energy change.
biophysics-nuclear-structure: Identify the nucleus Atomic number Z counts protons; mass number A counts protons plus neutrons. Isotopes share Z but differ in neutron number. Nuclear stability reflects competing interactions and neutron–proton balance; binding energy per nucleon helps compare nuclear configurations. Atomic chemistry and nuclear transformation are distinct processes. Balance charged-particle decay Alpha emission lowers A by 4 and Z by 2. In beta-minus decay a neutron becomes a proton with an electron and antineutrino emitted, leaving A unchanged and increasing Z by 1. Beta-plus decay lowers Z by 1 with a positron and neutrino emitted; electron capture also lowers Z by 1. Separate de-excitation Gamma emission releases nuclear excitation energy without changing A or Z. A daughter may remain excited after another decay and subsequently emit gamma radiation. Beta spectra are continuous because energy is shared with another emitted particle; many alpha and gamma emissions have characteristic discrete energies. Explain production Radionuclides can be produced by nuclear reactions in reactors or accelerators, or obtained from decay of a parent in a generator. The daughter element follows charge and nucleon bookkeeping. Production route, chemical separation, purity and half-life all influence whether a radionuclide is useful as a tracer. Work nuclear bookkeeping An alpha decay of a nucleus with A = 226 and Z = 88 produces a daughter with A = 222 and Z = 86. A following gamma emission leaves those numbers unchanged. Do not subtract four electrons or interpret a gamma photon as a lost nucleon.
biophysics-light-duality: Separate the experiments Interference reveals wave behaviour; the photoelectric effect reveals quantised energy exchange. Increasing light intensity increases photon arrival rate at a fixed frequency. Increasing frequency increases each photon's energy. One description is not a licence to use a classical wave-energy argument for the photoelectric threshold. Apply the photoelectric equation The maximum emitted electron kinetic energy is Kmax = hf − φ, where φ is the material's work function. Below threshold hf < φ, increasing intensity does not produce ordinary single-photon photoemission. Above threshold, intensity mainly changes the number of emitted electrons, not their maximum kinetic energy. Compare matter waves A particle with momentum p has de Broglie wavelength λ = h/p. Electron diffraction demonstrates that this relation is experimentally meaningful. Electron microscopes use accelerated electrons and electromagnetic lenses; their short wavelengths permit high resolution, but specimen preparation, lens aberrations and beam damage constrain useful detail. Work a photon example Using hc ≈ 1240 eV·nm, a 400 nm photon carries 3.10 eV. If the work function is 2.00 eV, the maximum photoelectron energy is 1.10 eV. Doubling photon flux doubles the potential event rate in an ideal unsaturated detector without changing this maximum energy. Connect momentum to force Light changes momentum when absorbed or redirected. Optical traps use focused-beam forces to confine suitable small particles; heating, particle refractive properties and geometry matter. The electromagnetic spectrum orders frequency and wavelength continuously: labels such as visible or X-ray do not introduce a new photon energy law.
biophysics-practical-absorbance: Establish the reference Measure a blank containing the appropriate solvent and container contribution. Then compare sample intensity I with blank intensity I₀. Use A = −log₁₀(I/I₀), taking transmission as a fraction rather than a percentage. A monochromator selects a wavelength range; it does not remove every instrumental error. Compare two samples Absorbance 1 means 10% transmission and absorbance 3 means 0.1%. The second transmits 100 times less light, although its absorbance is only three times as large. Under Beer–Lambert assumptions, concentration is proportional to absorbance at fixed wavelength and path length. Work a dilution A fivefold diluted sample has A = 0.40, and the calibration gives concentration 2 units per absorbance unit. Diluted concentration is 0.80 units; original concentration is 4.0 units. Apply the dilution factor after using the calibration, and keep concentration units consistent. Recognise failed assumptions Stray light, turbidity, chemical changes and detector limits can bend a calibration. A reading beyond the validated range should prompt suitable dilution or method review. A blank cannot make a scattering suspension behave like an ideal clear solution.
biophysics-practical-diffusion: Choose the observed quantity For one-dimensional free diffusion, ⟨x²⟩ = 2Dt, so a mean-squared-displacement versus time slope estimates 2D. A concentration profile requires a different fit and suitable boundary conditions. Individual trajectories fluctuate; one displacement is not the ensemble average. Work a scale With D = 2 × 10⁻¹⁰ m²/s and t = 1 s, root-mean-square displacement is √(2Dt) = 2 × 10⁻⁵ m, or 20 μm. At 4 s it is 40 μm. The distance grows with the square root of time, not linearly. Test the interpretation Drift adds directed motion and can make a simple diffusion estimate misleading. Temperature, viscosity, particle size, confinement and binding also matter. In an optical concentration experiment, converting signal into concentration introduces calibration uncertainty before the transport model is fitted. Compare transport routes Convection carries material with bulk flow; diffusion reflects random motion and concentration redistribution. A membrane may add a permeability barrier rather than merely extending a free-fluid distance. State which region and transport mechanism the measured coefficient describes.
biophysics-practical-biosignals: Read calibration first An ECG trace needs both voltage and paper-speed calibration. At 10 mm/mV, a 12 mm deflection represents 1.2 mV. At 25 mm/s, a 2 mm interval is 0.08 s. These are measurement exercises; voltage or timing alone is insufficient for a clinical interpretation. Compare leads and rejection Standard limb leads obey II = I + III in the ideal consistent-sign description. Differential amplifiers measure a voltage difference and aim to reject common-mode interference. Poor contact and motion can still introduce artifacts; a large recorded deflection need not reflect a larger cardiac source. Classify pulse behaviour An astable circuit oscillates without a stable resting state, a monostable returns to its stable state after a triggered pulse, and a bistable has two stable states. These concepts help explain timing electronics. A conceptual pulse exercise is not an instruction to construct or program a pacemaker. Work a pulse train A period of 1 s gives frequency 1 Hz. A pulse lasting 2 ms every second has duty cycle 0.2%. For an ideal rectangular voltage pulse across a resistor, energy is V²t/R. Shape, load and safety controls matter in real devices, so this ideal expression is used only for the classroom model.
biophysics-practical-coulter: Explain the aperture In a Coulter-type measurement, particles suspended in conducting electrolyte pass through a small aperture. A particle displaces conducting liquid and changes electrical resistance, producing a pulse. Under calibrated conditions, pulse size relates to displaced volume, while pulse count relates to the number of detected passages. Control the suspension An appropriate electrolyte and suspension preserve meaningful particle behaviour. Dilution reduces the chance that two particles occupy the sensing region together. Debris, aggregation and particles outside the calibrated range can distort a distribution; the instrument does not identify every cell type from volume alone. Work a dilution correction A diluted sample yields 200 counted particles per μL after the instrument's volume calculation. With a 100-fold dilution, the original estimate is 20,000 per μL. This assumes representative mixing, correct sampled volume and negligible unresolved coincidence. Interpret coincidence Two cells passing together may generate one larger event, biasing both count and apparent size. Lowering concentration can test whether coincidence contributes. A histogram peak is a population pattern, not proof that every event represents one normal cell.
biophysics-practical-eye: Use a simplified eye The eye's combined optical power is often approximated near 60 D, with a major contribution from the cornea. Accommodation changes lens shape and power. This reduced-eye model is useful for reasoning but does not capture every refracting surface or individual variation. Locate the focus In myopia, parallel rays focus in front of the retina in the uncorrected relaxed eye; a diverging correction reduces effective convergence. In hyperopia, the relaxed focus would lie behind the retina; a converging correction can help. Presbyopia concerns reduced accommodation rather than being identical to either axial refractive error. Interpret acuity Acuity tests assess the smallest resolvable angular detail under defined conditions. If minimum resolvable angle is 2 arcminutes, decimal acuity under the conventional reciprocal relation is 0.5. Viewing distance, contrast and correct use of the chart matter; an acuity value alone does not measure all aspects of vision. Explain the blind spot The optic disc lacks photoreceptors where the nerve exits. A target can disappear at the corresponding visual-field position despite intact surrounding vision. This is anatomically different from optical blur caused by defocus, and it is not the same structure as the fovea.
biophysics-practical-amplifiers: Define the ratio Voltage gain is output voltage divided by input voltage. For a voltage ratio, gain in decibels is 20 log₁₀|Vout/Vin|; interpreting that as power gain requires appropriate impedance conditions. Power ratios use 10 log₁₀(Pout/Pin). A decibel value needs its reference and quantity. Read a frequency response Amplifier gain can vary with frequency. Bandwidth identifies a useful range under a stated criterion, commonly relative to a midband level. Negative feedback can improve stability and linearity while changing gain and bandwidth. It cannot recover information already clipped at an earlier stage. Work a gain A 2 mV input becomes 200 mV, giving voltage gain 100 and 40 dB. A further stage with gain 10 gives total gain 1000, or 60 dB. Linear gains multiply, while their decibel values add when defined consistently. Check clipping and loading A signal that exceeds available output range clips, distorting the waveform and adding spectral components. A voltage divider's output also changes when a load draws current. Write down input range, output limit and loading assumptions before treating an amplifier as a perfect multiplier.
biophysics-practical-attenuation: Define attenuation quantities For a narrow monoenergetic beam in a uniform material, I/I₀ = exp(−μx). Linear attenuation coefficient μ has inverse-length units. Mass attenuation coefficient μ/ρ separates density, and areal density ρx has mass-per-area units. Absorption and removal from the direct beam are not identical. Use layer definitions Half-value layer is ln 2/μ; tenth-value layer is ln 10/μ. Two half-value layers leave one quarter and three leave one eighth. For a broad polyenergetic beam, scatter and beam hardening can prevent a single constant half-value layer from describing every depth. Work thickness If the half-value layer is 2 cm in the stated model, reducing direct intensity to 1/16 requires four layers, or 8 cm. This is a mathematical teaching example, not a shielding design specification. Actual shielding depends on the spectrum, geometry and regulatory context. Compare materials fairly Lead attenuation varies with photon energy; it has no universal percentage reduction per millimetre. Water and steam at the same thickness have different areal densities. At equal composition and appropriate energy, using mass thickness clarifies why density changes the linear attenuation.
biophysics-practical-lenses: Set up the measurement Record focal length in metres before using P = 1/f. For image distance, state the thin-lens sign convention and place object, lens and focal points on a sketch. The 17 mm focal length of a simplified optical system corresponds to about 58.8 D, not 0.0588 D. Calibrate the eyepiece An eyepiece scale has arbitrary divisions until compared with a stage micrometer. If 40 eyepiece divisions span 100 μm, each division represents 2.5 μm for that objective and configuration. Changing the objective requires a new calibration; changing magnification is not a licence to reuse the old conversion. Work an unknown length A structure spanning 12 calibrated divisions is 30 μm in this example. Repeat measurements across suitable boundaries and report meaningful precision. A thick or oblique section can change apparent size independently of the optical calibration. Predict before calculating For a converging lens, an object beyond twice the focal length produces a reduced real image. Between one and two focal lengths it produces an enlarged real image. Inside the focal length it produces a virtual enlarged image; exactly at the focus is the parallel-ray limiting case.
biophysics-practical-polarimetry: Prepare a polarised reference A polariser produces a defined polarisation state; an analyser compares the emerging orientation. Optical activity rotates the plane of linearly polarised light in suitable chiral media. Linear, circular and elliptical polarisation describe field evolution, not different photon charges. State Biot's relation For suitable conditions, rotation α = [α]lc, with specific rotation [α], path length l and concentration c in the convention used by the calibration. Temperature and wavelength must be specified. Opposite enantiomers can rotate equally in opposite directions; a racemic mixture may cancel net rotation. Work a path change A sample rotates light by +8° in a 1 dm cell. Under the same conditions, a 2 dm cell gives +16°. If concentration also halves, the rotation returns to +8°. Keep the sign because clockwise and counterclockwise rotations should not be reduced to unsigned brightness values. Interpret a null result Zero net rotation does not prove that no chiral molecules are present. Opposite contributions may cancel, concentration may be too low, or the measurement may be unsuitable. A polarimeter alone also does not determine a molecule's complete three-dimensional structure.
biophysics-practical-oscillations: Start with an ideal oscillator For a mass on an ideal spring, f = (1/2π)√(k/m). Displacement, velocity and acceleration have related but different phases. The model requires small motion in a linear spring regime; a biological structure may be nonlinear or have several modes. Add damping and driving Damping dissipates mechanical energy and reduces free-oscillation amplitude. Periodic forcing produces a frequency-dependent response, with resonance shaped by damping. Greater damping usually broadens and lowers the resonance peak. Resonance does not mean a device produces energy without external input. Work a change Doubling mass at fixed k multiplies frequency by 1/√2 ≈ 0.707. Doubling k at fixed mass multiplies frequency by √2. A cantilever can act as a mechanical sensor because changes in effective stiffness or mass affect its oscillation response. Read a decay curve An exponentially decaying amplitude should not be confused with the energy envelope: in a simple harmonic mode, energy scales with amplitude squared. A halved amplitude therefore corresponds to one quarter of the oscillation energy under the same stiffness.
biophysics-practical-refractometry: Identify the principle An Abbe refractometer relates a boundary angle to sample refractive index using prisms of known optical properties. The light–dark boundary is a measurement feature, not a molecular image. Dispersion compensation helps compare wavelengths when using suitable illumination. Control the conditions Refractive index depends on wavelength, temperature and composition. A concentration estimate therefore requires a calibration for the relevant mixture under matching conditions. A water reference is not a universal constant equal to exactly one; that value is approximately for air relative to vacuum. Use a calibration Suppose a validated local calibration is n = 1.333 + 0.0015c with c in the calibration's stated concentration units. A reading of 1.348 gives c = (1.348 − 1.333)/0.0015 = 10 units. The numerical relation cannot be transferred to an unrelated solute without evidence. Judge the uncertainty A temperature drift or poorly defined boundary can shift the reading without a true concentration change. Record the calibration, temperature and wavelength specification with the result. For a nonlinear calibration curve, interpolate within the measured range rather than extrapolating a straight line indefinitely.
