Separate mixing, propulsion and absorption Segmentation mainly mixes intestinal contents and increases contact with the mucosa, whereas coordinated peristalsis produces forward propulsion. Digestion breaks macromolecules into absorbable components; absorption moves those components across the epithelium. Pancreatic enzymes, bile-mediated lipid handling and membrane transport each contribute different steps. Explain how a meal containing fat and acid can recruit different pancreatic responses. Duodenal acid stimulates secretin and bicarbonate-rich ductal secretion. Fat and protein products stimulate cholecystokinin and enzyme-rich secretion, with neural signals coordinating the response. The pathways interact rather than operating as isolated switches. Fat enters the duodenum. Which coordinated response fits its digestion? CCK supporting enzyme secretion and gallbladder contraction. CCK helps match enzyme and bile delivery to the incoming nutrient load.
ecg-time-and-vectors: Keep the electrical and mechanical stories separate The ECG records changing voltage differences at the body surface. The P wave reflects atrial depolarisation, the QRS complex ventricular depolarisation and the T wave ventricular repolarisation. Atrial repolarisation is usually obscured by the much larger QRS. These are electrical events that precede or overlap mechanical events. A QRS complex is not itself a measurement of ejection or stroke volume, and an electrical tracing alone does not establish effective blood flow. Read the calibration first At a paper speed of 25 mm/s, one 1-mm small square represents 0.04 s and one 5-mm large square represents 0.20 s. At 50 mm/s the same distances represent half those times. Standard voltage calibration is often 10 mm/mV, but it must be checked rather than assumed. For a regular rhythm, heart rate in beats/min = 60 / R–R interval in seconds. Counting large squares with the 300 rule only applies at 25 mm/s. Define the interval endpoints The PR interval starts at P-wave onset and ends at QRS onset. It includes atrial depolarisation and conduction toward the ventricles; it is not simply the duration of the AV node alone. The PR segment begins after the P wave ends. QRS duration measures ventricular depolarisation. The QT interval extends from QRS onset to T-wave end and includes ventricular depolarisation and repolarisation. QT varies with rate, so a raw interval is not interpreted independently of heart rate. Project the vector onto a lead A lead has a positive and a negative direction. A net depolarisation vector toward its positive electrode produces an upward deflection; a vector pointing away produces a downward deflection. A nearly perpendicular vector can produce a small or biphasic signal. The same activation can therefore look different in different leads. Limb leads sample the frontal plane and chest leads the horizontal plane. Begin with calibration, rate, regularity, P-to-QRS relationship and intervals before making an interpretation. Relate P, QRS and T to electrical events. Convert ECG grid distances into time and rate. Predict how a lead records a depolarisation vector. Read a calibrated strip A fictional regular tracing at 25 mm/s has four large squares between successive R peaks and four small squares from P onset to QRS onset. Calculate rate and PR interval. R–R = 4 × 0.20 = 0.80 s. Rate = 60 / 0.80 = 75 beats/min. PR = 4 × 0.04 = 0.16 s. If the speed were 50 mm/s, the same distances would instead represent 150 beats/min and 0.08 s. Calibration is essential.
endocrine-feedback: Name the three levels In the hypothalamic–pituitary–thyroid axis, hypothalamic TRH supports pituitary TSH release, and TSH stimulates the thyroid. Thyroid hormones then act on many target tissues. Drawing the levels separately helps distinguish a gland's response to stimulation from the actions of its hormone elsewhere in the body. Close the feedback loop Thyroid hormone feeds back on the hypothalamus and pituitary, reducing stimulation when hormone availability rises. Feedback is a regulatory relationship, not simply a label attached to every endocrine pathway. Some hormones use different controlling variables, and secretion can be pulsatile or follow daily rhythms. Explain a simplified pattern In a simplified primary thyroid-gland failure model, reduced thyroid hormone removes inhibitory feedback and TSH rises if the pituitary can respond. If the defect instead lies centrally, TSH may be low or inappropriately normal despite low thyroid hormone. Real interpretation requires clinical context, assay limitations and other influences; this example teaches the feedback logic. Explain why a target-gland hormone and its pituitary signal can move in opposite directions. A target-gland hormone can inhibit its upstream control signals. When target-gland secretion falls, reduced negative feedback permits the pituitary signal to rise, provided the central components of the axis remain functional. Low thyroid hormone is accompanied by a TSH that is not appropriately elevated. What does this challenge in a simple model? The assumption that the central feedback response is intact. An intact pituitary response to primary thyroid failure would usually raise TSH; central influences merit consideration.
energy-balance: Use a conservation statement Over a defined interval, the change in stored body energy reflects absorbed energy intake minus energy expenditure. Expenditure includes basal cellular work, physical activity and the thermic effect of food. Body mass also changes with water and gastrointestinal contents, so a short-term weight change is not a direct measurement of a change in fat energy. Connect the fed state to storage After a mixed meal, insulin supports storage and use of absorbed nutrients. Glucose can enter insulin-responsive tissues, glycogen stores can be replenished, and lipid storage is favoured. The exact response depends on tissue transporters and metabolic pathways; not every tissue requires insulin for glucose uptake. Connect fasting to mobilisation As the interval since eating increases, a lower insulin-to-glucagon signal supports hepatic glucose production and mobilisation of stored fuels. Glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis contribute on different time scales, while fatty acids supply many tissues. Hormonal control redistributes available fuels; it does not create energy from nothing. Compare nutrient handling after a meal and during fasting. The fed state favours use and storage of absorbed nutrients under a higher insulin signal. Fasting promotes mobilisation of stored fuels and hepatic glucose production under a lower insulin-to-glucagon signal. Energy is transferred and transformed, not created. Which statement best connects fasting to ongoing cellular work? Stored substrates are mobilised to support continued metabolism. Fasting changes fuel sources while tissues continue to use energy.
renal-kidney-map: Two paths, one organ Blood enters a glomerulus through an afferent arteriole and leaves through an efferent arteriole. A second capillary bed receives that blood: peritubular capillaries around cortical tubules, or vasa recta associated with juxtamedullary nephrons. Filtrate crosses into Bowman space and takes a different route through the tubules. Four verbs that keep the map straight Filtration moves fluid and small solutes from glomerular blood into Bowman space. Reabsorption returns material from tubular fluid to blood. Secretion moves material from blood into tubular fluid. Excretion is what finally leaves in urine: filtered amount minus reabsorbed amount plus secreted amount. Location explains function Renal corpuscles lie in the cortex. Long loops of juxtamedullary nephrons extend into the medulla and help establish the concentration gradient. Collecting ducts receive fluid from multiple nephrons and use that gradient when their water permeability increases. Trace the two capillary beds in series. Separate filtration, reabsorption, secretion and excretion. Locate the cortex, medulla and collecting system.
blood-and-haemostasis: Anchor platelets at an injured surface Vascular injury exposes adhesive structures and immobilised von Willebrand factor. Platelet GPIb-IX-V binds von Willebrand factor, while collagen receptors help stabilise adhesion. Platelets then change shape, release mediators and recruit further platelets. Adhesion attaches a platelet to the injured surface; it is not the same event as platelet-to-platelet aggregation. Connect platelets to one another Activation changes the affinity of integrin alpha-IIb-beta-3, also called GPIIb/IIIa. Fibrinogen can bridge these receptors on neighbouring platelets. ADP, thromboxane and thrombin help amplify activation. Platelets also expose a phospholipid surface that supports coagulation-complex assembly, linking primary and secondary haemostasis. Amplify thrombin and stabilise fibrin Intrinsic tenase contains factor IXa with its cofactor VIIIa on a calcium-dependent phospholipid surface; it activates factor X. Factor Xa with Va forms prothrombinase, producing thrombin from prothrombin. Thrombin converts fibrinogen to fibrin, and factor XIIIa crosslinks fibrin. These overlapping processes stabilise the plug; they are not two completely separate timelines. Explain the difference between adhesion, aggregation and fibrin stabilisation. Adhesion anchors platelets to an injured surface. Aggregation joins activated platelets through fibrinogen bridges between alpha-IIb-beta-3 receptors. Coagulation generates thrombin and fibrin, and factor XIIIa crosslinks fibrin to stabilise the plug. A student confuses prothrombinase with intrinsic tenase. Which reaction belongs to prothrombinase? Prothrombin to thrombin. Xa with Va forms prothrombinase and supports thrombin generation.
renal-concentrating-urine: Build the gradient Countercurrent multiplication in the loops of Henle helps establish the corticomedullary osmotic gradient. The descending thin limb permits substantial water movement; the ascending limb recovers salt while restricting water movement. Urea recycling contributes to inner medullary osmolality. Preserve the gradient Vasa recta exchange limits the removal of medullary solute while supplying tissue. Excessive washout weakens the gradient. Countercurrent exchange preserves a gradient; it is not the same mechanism as multiplication in the loop. Open the water route ADH acts on basolateral V2 receptors of collecting-duct principal cells. Gs, cAMP and PKA signaling increases apical AQP2 insertion. Water then moves down an osmotic gradient. With little ADH, low collecting-duct water permeability permits more dilute urine; with ADH and an intact gradient, more water is recovered. Distinguish countercurrent multiplication and exchange. Locate the V2 receptor and AQP2. Explain why ADH needs an intact medullary gradient.
renal-abg-interpretation: Start with pH, but do not stop there For these teaching cases, the arterial pH reference interval is 7.35–7.45, PaCO₂ 35–45 mmHg and bicarbonate 22–26 mmol/L. Acidemia and alkalemia describe the measured pH. Acidosis and alkalosis describe processes: mixed processes may coexist even when pH is inside the reference interval. Read the ratio pH = 6.1 + log₁₀[HCO₃⁻ / (0.03 × PaCO₂)]. A primary fall in bicarbonate drives metabolic acidosis; a primary rise in CO₂ drives respiratory acidosis. The opposite changes drive alkalosis. Compensation moves pH toward the baseline; it should not be assumed simply because both measurements are abnormal. Test the explanation For metabolic acidosis, Winter’s formula gives an expected PaCO₂ of 1.5 × HCO₃⁻ + 8, with a ±2 mmHg range. A measured value above the range suggests an additional respiratory acidosis; below suggests an additional respiratory alkalosis. Also calculate Na⁺ − (Cl⁻ + HCO₃⁻); interpret this anion gap against the laboratory range and albumin. Neither a gap nor an ABG alone establishes a cause. Distinguish acidemia from an acidosis process. Identify the primary change in simple examples. Use expected compensation to recognize a possible additional process.
indicator-dilution: Begin with conservation of the indicator A known amount of indicator is placed into an unknown fluid volume. After mixing, concentration equals the amount remaining divided by that volume. Rearranging gives volume = amount remaining / equilibrated concentration. The indicator should mix throughout the compartment of interest, remain measurable and avoid appreciable entry into other compartments during the measurement. The calculation measures the distribution space of the tracer; naming that space requires understanding its behaviour. Match the tracer to the compartment Labelled water can distribute across cell membranes and therefore estimates total body water. An extracellular marker that is largely excluded from cells estimates extracellular fluid. An indicator retained with plasma proteins estimates plasma volume. Intracellular fluid is usually derived as total body water minus extracellular fluid. Interstitial fluid is approximately extracellular fluid minus plasma volume; whether small transcellular spaces are included depends on the tracer and measurement convention. Correct the numerator before dividing If an indicator is excreted or otherwise lost before the equilibrium sample, subtract that loss from the administered amount. Dividing the full administered amount by a concentration already reduced by loss overestimates volume. Concentration must use units compatible with the dose: milligrams divided by milligrams per litre gives litres. A concentration in milligrams per millilitre instead gives millilitres. Do the unit cancellation explicitly before deciding whether an answer is plausible. Interpret the estimate rather than memorising a person The familiar total-body-water fraction is an illustrative average, not a constant for every person. Body composition and age alter the fractions. A result may also be distorted by sampling before complete mixing, indicator leakage or uncorrected disappearance. Subtraction combines the uncertainty of two measurements. Blood volume and plasma volume are different: in a simplified model, blood volume = plasma volume / (1 − haematocrit), with haematocrit expressed as a fraction. Choose a tracer from the barrier it can cross. Calculate compartment volume after correcting indicator loss. Distinguish measured volume from a volume found by subtraction. A loss-corrected measurement A fictional extracellular tracer dose is 150 mg. By sampling, 10 mg has been lost and the equilibrated concentration is 10 mg/L. Total body water was measured separately as 42 L. Find extracellular and intracellular volumes. Remaining tracer = 150 − 10 = 140 mg. Extracellular volume = 140 mg / 10 mg/L = 14 L. Intracellular volume = 42 − 14 = 28 L. Using 150 mg would give 15 L and overestimate extracellular volume by 1 L.
lymph-and-fluid-exchange: Separate pressure from permeability Capillary hydrostatic pressure favours outward fluid movement. Plasma proteins contribute an opposing colloid osmotic effect, but the endothelial barrier and its glycocalyx determine how those forces act. A pressure change alone does not fully describe exchange when permeability or protein distribution also changes. Include the lymphatic route Lymphatic vessels return filtered interstitial fluid and proteins to the circulation. Sustained venous-end reabsorption is not a universal feature of all systemic capillaries. In many tissues, lymphatic return handles much of the net filtration. Different organs have specialised exchange arrangements, so one diagram should not be treated as a universal map. Build an oedema mechanism Oedema can result when filtration exceeds the capacity for return. Increased venous pressure, increased permeability, reduced plasma protein concentration or impaired lymphatic drainage can contribute through different mechanisms. In a teaching explanation, specify which part changed and then trace its effect; appearance alone does not establish a cause. Explain how venous pressure and lymphatic obstruction can both produce fluid accumulation. Higher venous pressure can increase capillary hydrostatic pressure and filtration. Lymphatic obstruction reduces the route that returns filtered fluid and proteins. Both can increase interstitial fluid, but through different parts of the balance. Two examples cause oedema: increased venous pressure and lymphatic obstruction. What differs? One can increase filtration; the other reduces return. They change different sides of the filtration–return balance.
synaptic-integration: Release a chemical signal An action potential reaching a presynaptic terminal opens voltage-gated calcium channels. Local calcium entry activates the vesicle-fusion machinery, allowing neurotransmitter release into the synaptic cleft. The transmitter then acts on postsynaptic receptors. Calcium links the arriving electrical event to release; it is not the transmitter crossing the cleft. Interpret the postsynaptic conductance change Ionotropic receptors directly regulate channel opening, whereas metabotropic receptors recruit intracellular signalling. Whether an input is excitatory or inhibitory depends on the conductance change, its reversal potential and the receiving cell's state. Inhibitory input can reduce excitability by shunting current even when the membrane does not become much more negative. Combine inputs in time and space Temporal summation combines inputs arriving close together in time. Spatial summation combines inputs from different locations. Dendritic filtering, synapse position and inhibitory conductance shape the result. An action potential is generated when the combined effect reaches the relevant threshold; a single postsynaptic potential need not cause a spike. An action potential and changing conductance Aligned graphs show a neuronal action potential, an early increase in relative sodium conductance and a later, longer potassium conductance increase. Read the two panels together: rapid sodium-channel activation accompanies the upstroke; sodium inactivation and delayed potassium-channel activation support repolarisation. Voltages, timing and conductances are illustrative and vary between cells. This neuronal waveform is not a universal muscle or pacemaker waveform. Distinguish chemical transmission from temporal and spatial summation. Chemical transmission releases a transmitter that changes postsynaptic signalling or conductance. Temporal summation combines closely timed inputs; spatial summation combines inputs at different sites. Their combined effect helps determine whether the receiving neuron fires. Repeated small inputs at the same synapse arrive close together and have a larger combined effect. What is this? Temporal summation. Temporal summation combines effects of closely timed inputs.
renal-renal-acid-base: Reclamation prevents a loss Much filtered bicarbonate is recovered in the proximal tubule. Secreted H⁺ combines with luminal bicarbonate; carbonic anhydrase supports conversion through CO₂ and water. Intracellular reactions permit bicarbonate to return to blood. Recovering filtered bicarbonate prevents its loss, but is not the same as adding new bicarbonate to the body. New bicarbonate needs net acid excretion Acid can leave the body buffered as ammonium or titratable acid, including phosphate-buffered H⁺. Net acid excretion is ammonium excretion plus titratable acid excretion minus urinary bicarbonate loss. Ammoniagenesis is an adaptable component of the renal response to an acid load. A final cellular choice Alpha intercalated cells secrete H⁺ into urine and return bicarbonate to blood. Beta intercalated cells can secrete bicarbonate. These renal adjustments complement lung regulation of CO₂, but full adaptation is slower than the immediate buffering response. Explain filtered bicarbonate reclamation. Connect ammonium and titratable acid excretion to new bicarbonate. Distinguish alpha and beta intercalated cells.
reproductive-cycles: Begin with a coordinated axis Pulsatile hypothalamic GnRH supports pituitary LH and FSH secretion. In the ovary, gonadotrophins support follicular development and steroid production. In the testis, LH supports Leydig-cell testosterone production, while FSH acts on Sertoli cells in support of spermatogenesis. The same pituitary signals act within different tissue arrangements. Connect follicular growth to ovulation Developing ovarian follicles produce estradiol. During most of the cycle, ovarian hormones contribute inhibitory feedback. Sustained sufficiently high estradiol near ovulation can instead generate positive feedback and an LH surge. The surge promotes final oocyte maturation, ovulation and luteinisation. A 28-day diagram is an illustration, not a schedule every person must follow. Match the endometrium to ovarian hormones Estradiol supports proliferative endometrial growth. After ovulation, the corpus luteum produces progesterone, promoting secretory differentiation. If pregnancy does not maintain luteal function, falling progesterone and estradiol contribute to menstruation. Fertilisation usually occurs in the uterine-tube ampulla; implantation is a later, distinct event in the uterus. Relate the ovarian and endometrial phases without assuming a fixed calendar. Follicular estradiol supports endometrial proliferation. A sustained estradiol rise can trigger an LH surge and ovulation. Luteal progesterone supports secretory endometrium; falling luteal hormones contribute to menstruation when pregnancy does not maintain the corpus luteum. After ovulation, which hormone most directly supports secretory differentiation of the endometrium? Progesterone from the corpus luteum. Luteal progesterone supports secretory changes following estradiol-driven proliferation.
membrane-potentials: Create the resting voltage Concentration gradients and selective permeability determine membrane potential. In many resting excitable cells, potassium permeability strongly influences the voltage. The sodium–potassium pump maintains the gradients and also has a smaller direct electrogenic effect. Cross threshold In a simplified neuronal model, depolarization opens voltage-gated sodium channels, producing regenerative inward current. An action potential is all-or-none for a given cell under specified conditions; stronger sustained stimulation is often encoded through frequency rather than endlessly larger spikes. Recover excitability Sodium-channel inactivation and delayed potassium current support repolarization. Recovery from inactivation underlies refractory behavior. Channel contributions differ among neurons, skeletal muscle, working cardiac cells and pacemaker cells; one waveform does not represent all excitable tissues. An action potential and changing conductance Aligned graphs show a neuronal action potential, an early increase in relative sodium conductance and a later, longer potassium conductance increase. Read the two panels together: rapid sodium-channel activation accompanies the upstroke; sodium inactivation and delayed potassium-channel activation support repolarisation. Voltages, timing and conductances are illustrative and vary between cells. This neuronal waveform is not a universal muscle or pacemaker waveform.
special-senses: Light reduces photoreceptor depolarisation In darkness, cyclic-GMP-dependent channels support the photoreceptor dark current. Light activates the phototransduction cascade, reducing cyclic GMP and closing these channels. The photoreceptor hyperpolarises and releases less glutamate. This is a graded receptor response; it is not a conventional all-or-none action potential in the rod or cone. Hair bundles gate a mechanically sensitive current Deflection of a sensory hair bundle in its excitatory direction opens mechanotransduction channels. Potassium-rich endolymph and the electrochemical arrangement favour an inward current that depolarises the hair cell. This changes calcium entry and transmitter release to sensory afferents. Deflection in the opposite direction reduces the response. Keep the sensory code and route separate Cochlear position helps encode sound frequency because different parts of the basilar membrane respond best to different frequencies. Vestibular organs instead contribute information about head movement and orientation. A complete explanation names the stimulus, receptor response, transmitter change and afferent pathway, rather than saying that every sensory receptor fires in the same way. Compare the direction of the initial receptor response to light and to excitatory hair-bundle deflection. Light closes cyclic-GMP-gated channels and hyperpolarises a photoreceptor. Excitatory hair-bundle deflection opens mechanically gated channels and depolarises a hair cell. Both graded responses regulate transmitter release. A hair bundle is deflected in its excitatory direction. Which initial response is expected? Opening of mechanotransduction channels and depolarisation. Mechanical channel opening permits a depolarising current under the inner-ear ionic conditions.
cardiac-output: Define each quantity Stroke volume is end-diastolic volume minus end-systolic volume. Cardiac output equals heart rate multiplied by stroke volume. Ejection fraction divides stroke volume by end-diastolic volume. The quantities describe different aspects of pumping and have different units. Change filling Increased venous return can increase end-diastolic filling and preload. Within physiological limits, length-dependent activation increases force and stroke volume: the Frank–Starling mechanism. This is not the same as an increase in intrinsic contractility. Change the pump state Contractility describes changes in force generation at a given starting length and loading context. Sympathetic beta1 signaling can increase inotropy. Afterload also affects ejection, so a change in ejection fraction cannot automatically be assigned to one mechanism. Compare ventricular pressure–volume loops Four qualitative left-ventricular pressure–volume panels compare the normal cycle and isolated changes in preload, afterload and contractility. Grey loops are the control. Compare width (stroke volume) and end-systolic position when one variable changes. These are isolated qualitative changes; physiological systems often change several variables together. The loops are not patient measurements.
baroreflex: Sense stretch Carotid-sinus and aortic-arch receptors respond to stretch associated with arterial pressure. Carotid signals travel predominantly through the glossopharyngeal pathway; aortic signals travel through the vagus. These are sensory inputs, not the final autonomic outputs. Integrate the change The medullary network, including nucleus tractus solitarius, adjusts autonomic activity. A rise in arterial pressure generally increases baroreceptor signaling, increases cardiac vagal influence and reduces sympathetic outflow. A fall produces the opposite compensatory tendency. Act on heart and vessels Changes in heart rate, contractility and vascular tone buffer the pressure disturbance. This is rapid feedback, not a complete account of long-term pressure control. Distinguish the arterial reflex from atrial stretch responses associated with increased venous return.
cardiac-cycle: Use pressure differences to order the cycle During filling, atrial pressure exceeds ventricular pressure and the atrioventricular valve is open. As ventricular pressure rises above atrial pressure, that valve closes. Before ventricular pressure exceeds arterial pressure, both valves are closed: pressure rises at almost constant volume. The arterial valve opens when the ventricular-to-arterial pressure difference favours ejection. Read the loop rather than its shape alone The width of a ventricular pressure–volume loop is stroke volume: end-diastolic minus end-systolic volume. Its area represents external stroke work. Isovolumetric contraction and relaxation are nearly vertical because volume changes little while pressure changes. Real measurements depend on loading conditions and valve function; a teaching loop simplifies these details. Change one variable at a time With other conditions held fixed, increased filling can raise stroke volume through the Frank–Starling mechanism. An isolated increase in afterload tends to increase end-systolic volume and reduce stroke volume on that beat. Increased contractility tends to reduce end-systolic volume. In an intact circulation, reflexes and subsequent filling can change the later response. Compare ventricular pressure–volume loops Four qualitative left-ventricular pressure–volume panels compare the normal cycle and isolated changes in preload, afterload and contractility. Grey loops are the control. Compare width (stroke volume) and end-systolic position when one variable changes. These are isolated qualitative changes; physiological systems often change several variables together. The loops are not patient measurements. Predict the immediate effect of an isolated afterload increase on a pressure–volume loop. At unchanged preload and contractility, the ventricle must develop more pressure before ejection. It generally ejects less on that beat, leaving a larger end-systolic volume and a narrower loop. Later reflex and filling responses may modify this. In a simplified ventricle, end-diastolic volume is 120 mL and end-systolic volume is 50 mL. What is stroke volume? 70 mL. Subtract end-systolic from end-diastolic volume: 120 minus 50 equals 70 mL.
muscle-contraction: Skeletal muscle: activate the thin filament At the neuromuscular junction, acetylcholine produces an end-plate depolarisation that can initiate a muscle action potential. In skeletal muscle, the T-tubule voltage sensor couples to sarcoplasmic-reticulum calcium release. Calcium binds troponin C, moving the tropomyosin constraint on actin–myosin interaction. ATP supports cross-bridge cycling and calcium reuptake. Cardiac muscle: trigger calcium-induced release In cardiac working myocytes, calcium entering through L-type channels triggers further calcium release from the sarcoplasmic reticulum. Troponin C again regulates the thin filament. The prolonged action potential and refractory period strongly limit summation into tetanus, allowing filling between contractions. This working-myocyte model differs from nodal pacemaker activity. Smooth muscle: regulate myosin Smooth muscle uses calcium–calmodulin to activate myosin light-chain kinase. Phosphorylation of myosin supports interaction with actin; myosin light-chain phosphatase favours relaxation. Smooth muscle lacks the troponin switch used in striated muscle. Stretch, local signals and autonomic input can regulate force, sometimes without a full action potential. Compare the role of calcium in skeletal, cardiac and smooth muscle. Skeletal and cardiac muscle use troponin C to regulate actin access. Skeletal coupling primarily releases stored calcium through voltage-sensor coupling; cardiac muscle needs trigger calcium entry. Smooth muscle uses calcium–calmodulin and myosin light-chain kinase to regulate myosin. Why can normal skeletal muscle produce tetanic force while normal cardiac working muscle cannot? The cardiac refractory period overlaps much of its contraction. The long refractory period limits repeated excitation and summation into tetanus, preserving filling between beats.
ventilation-perfusion: Deliver air and blood Ventilation brings fresh gas to alveoli; perfusion brings blood to pulmonary capillaries. Effective exchange depends on their regional matching. Minute ventilation includes dead-space ventilation, so it does not directly equal fresh gas reaching exchange surfaces. Compare the limiting patterns Very low ventilation relative to perfusion approaches a shunt-like pattern. Ventilation without perfusion is dead space. These are different ways to waste one side of the exchange system; neither is explained solely by membrane thickness. Add diffusion and transport Gas crosses the barrier down partial-pressure gradients. Surface area, diffusion distance and gas properties affect transfer. Oxygen content then depends strongly on hemoglobin as well as saturation and dissolved oxygen; a partial pressure is not itself a complete oxygen-content measurement. Conducting airways and gas-exchanging alveoli Conducting airways are coloured red, alveoli blue; an inset shows surrounding capillaries and a conceptual oxygen and nitrogen washout graph. The conducting zone carries gas; gas exchange begins in the respiratory zone. In the source’s washout key, horizontal position means exhaled volume and vertical position means relative gas concentration. The solid red oxygen-rich signal falls while the dashed blue nitrogen signal rises after breathing oxygen. The graph is qualitative, without calibrated axes; do not use it to calculate dead-space volume.
respiratory-mechanics: Create a pressure gradient During quiet inspiration, diaphragm contraction expands the thorax. Alveolar pressure transiently falls below atmospheric pressure, so air flows inward. Airflow stops when the pressures equalise. Quiet expiration is mainly driven by elastic recoil. The diaphragm receives motor supply through the phrenic nerves, principally from C3–C5. Distinguish pressure from resistance For a simplified airway, airflow equals the pressure difference divided by airway resistance. At the same pressure difference, doubling resistance halves airflow. Use this relationship to interpret the pressure diagram and resistance question below. Subtract the non-exchanging volume Minute ventilation equals tidal volume multiplied by respiratory rate. Alveolar ventilation is approximated by (tidal volume minus dead-space volume) multiplied by rate, using consistent units. Anatomic dead space is conducting-airway volume; alveolar dead space is ventilation that receives little or no effective perfusion. Compare two fictional breathing patterns With a fixed dead space of 150 mL, 500 mL breaths at 12/min give 4.2 L/min alveolar ventilation. Breaths of 300 mL at 20/min give only 3.0 L/min, despite the same 6.0 L/min minute ventilation. This is a simplified teaching calculation. Actual dead space and carbon-dioxide production vary; these examples are not ventilation prescriptions. Conducting airways and gas-exchanging alveoli Conducting airways are coloured red, alveoli blue; an inset shows surrounding capillaries and a conceptual oxygen and nitrogen washout graph. The conducting zone carries gas; gas exchange begins in the respiratory zone. In the source’s washout key, horizontal position means exhaled volume and vertical position means relative gas concentration. The solid red oxygen-rich signal falls while the dashed blue nitrogen signal rises after breathing oxygen. The graph is qualitative, without calibrated axes; do not use it to calculate dead-space volume. Explain why rapid shallow breaths can be less efficient than slower deeper breaths at the same minute ventilation. A fixed conducting-airway volume takes up more of each small breath. After subtracting dead space, less fresh air reaches gas-exchanging alveoli each minute, even when total minute ventilation is unchanged. At the same 6 L/min minute ventilation and a fixed 150 mL dead space, which pattern gives greater alveolar ventilation? 500 mL at 12 breaths/min. This gives (500−150)×12 = 4.2 L/min, because less of total ventilation is wasted in dead space.
renal-volume-and-osmolality: How much versus how concentrated Extracellular volume is closely linked to total body sodium content. Osmolality describes the number of dissolved particles relative to water. Plasma sodium concentration therefore reflects the relationship between solute and water, rather than directly measuring total sodium stores or circulating volume. Respond to low effective circulation Reduced renal perfusion, low NaCl delivery at the macula densa and renal sympathetic β1 stimulation can promote renin release. Angiotensin II supports vascular tone, sodium recovery, thirst and aldosterone secretion. Effective circulating volume describes how adequately the arterial circulation is filled, not merely the amount of fluid visible in tissues. Choose the hormone by the job Aldosterone increases distal sodium recovery and supports potassium secretion. ADH chiefly regulates collecting-duct water permeability. Increased osmolality stimulates thirst and ADH; a substantial fall in effective circulating volume can also stimulate ADH, even when osmotic signals would otherwise suppress it. Distinguish extracellular volume from concentration. Identify signals for renin release. Contrast aldosterone and ADH actions.
renal-water-balance: Identify the regulated variable Osmolality describes the concentration of osmotically active particles, whereas extracellular volume reflects the amount of fluid in that compartment. Sodium balance is a major determinant of extracellular volume; water balance strongly influences osmolality. The two variables interact, but an explanation should identify which change is driving the response. Use ADH to alter water permeability ADH binds basolateral V2 receptors on collecting-duct principal cells and promotes insertion of aquaporin-2 into the apical membrane. Water can then move into the hyperosmotic medullary interstitium. ADH uses the gradient; it does not create the entire countercurrent system by itself. Both osmotic signals and sufficiently strong volume signals can regulate its release. Use aldosterone to adjust sodium and potassium handling Aldosterone promotes sodium reabsorption and potassium secretion in responsive distal nephron cells by altering transport proteins, including epithelial sodium channels and the sodium–potassium ATPase. Angiotensin II and plasma potassium are important regulators. Predicting water retention additionally requires attention to water permeability, intake and the other control systems. Distinguish what ADH changes from what aldosterone changes. ADH increases collecting-duct water permeability through aquaporin-2 trafficking. Aldosterone enhances distal sodium reabsorption and potassium secretion. Their effects interact with medullary gradients, intake and circulating-volume signals. ADH rises, but the medullary osmotic gradient is greatly reduced. What limits water recovery? Increased permeability still needs an osmotic driving force. ADH makes a pathway available; the medullary gradient supplies the driving force.
renal-filtration-and-clearance: A virtual volume, not a drained container Clearance is the volume of plasma that would contain the amount of a substance excreted each minute. C = U × V / P. If urine concentration is 100 mg/mL, urine flow is 1 mL/min and plasma concentration is 1 mg/mL, clearance is 100 mL/min. The concentrations must use matching units. Choose the marker by its handling Inulin is freely filtered and neither reabsorbed nor secreted, so its clearance equals GFR under ideal measurement conditions. Creatinine is convenient but is also secreted slightly, so measured creatinine clearance tends to overestimate GFR. At low concentrations, PAH is filtered and strongly secreted; its clearance approximates effective renal plasma flow, because extraction is high but incomplete. Ask what the denominator contains Filtration fraction is GFR divided by renal plasma flow. For GFR 120 mL/min and RPF 600 mL/min, FF is 0.20, or 20%. Blood flow includes cells: RBF = RPF / (1 − hematocrit). Using PAH clearance in place of true RPF gives an estimate based on effective plasma flow. Calculate clearance from urine concentration, flow and plasma concentration. Explain why inulin, creatinine and PAH give different information. Calculate filtration fraction without confusing blood and plasma flow.
